title: Benchmarking quantum simulation at scale
authors: Jeremy Hartse, Mohsin Raza, Shravan Shravan, Ivan H. Deutsch, Niklas Mueller
abstract: The applications for which quantum computers will clearly outperform classical computers are still being identified and benchmarking such an advantage is challenging. We propose a scalable verification scheme for non-equilibrium quantum simulation based on stabilizer scars, a special class of quantum many-body scars, whose structure ensures both classical simulability and efficient direct fidelity estimation. Assuming a physically motivated error model, we show that the fidelity of quantum simulating these states bounds the fidelity of classically intractable simulations, providing a benchmark for quantum-advantage experiments in non-equilibrium dynamics.
summary: This paper introduces a novel benchmarking protocol for non-equilibrium quantum simulation using 'quantum many-body scars.' By restricting the simulation fidelity measurement to a special, classically simulable subspace, the authors create a quantifiable benchmark. This allows researchers to test if quantum hardware can simulate dynamics that are intractable for classical computers.
main_problem: The authors propose a scalable verification scheme for non-equilibrium quantum simulation to benchmark performance beyond classical computational limits.
main_result: They show that fidelity estimation within the specialized 'scar subspace' provides a quantifiable benchmark against the full Hilbert space, even under local depolarizing noise.
method: The protocol uses Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) applied to states confined to a quantum many-body scar subspace, leveraging stabilizer properties for efficient measurement scaling.
model_or_system: The study utilizes an Ising model on $n=2L$ qubits with periodic boundary conditions. The key feature is the existence of a polynomially large 'scar subspace' embedded in the exponentially large Hilbert space.
key_observables: Fidelity ($F$), Stabilizer Rényi entropy ($\mathcal{M}_\alpha$), and expectation values of Pauli observables ($	ext{Tr}[ho W_k]$).
important_parameters: Local depolarizing noise strength ($p$), system size ($L$ or $n$), and required measurement precision ($\epsilon, \delta$).
main_assumptions: The dominant error is approximated by local depolarizing noise, and the method relies on the existence of a polynomially large scar subspace.
figures_summary: Figures compare fidelities in the full vs. scar subspaces under noise (Fig 2), demonstrate MCMC estimation accuracy independent of system size (Fig 3a), and show how shot counts affect statistical uncertainty estimates (Fig S4).
paper_structure: The paper develops a three-part benchmarking protocol: defining the QMBS, showing DFE efficiency via stabilizer entropy bounds, and deriving quantitative relationships between scar and full-space fidelities under noise.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, mathematically rigorous framework for testing quantum advantage in dynamics by isolating measurable quantities (fidelity) that are sensitive to computational hardness.
